documentation.range:
Lophius piscatorius is distributed from zero to 600 m depth from the southwestern Barents Sea to the Strait of Gibraltar (Caruso 1986), as well as throughout the Mediterranean Sea, and south to Mauritania (Caruso in press). This species was described as frequently occurring in a trawl survey conducted off the coast of Namibia between the years 1992-1996 (Hamukuaya et al. 2001), but this record from Namibia may be a misidentification of Lophius budegassa. Vakily et al. (2002) report L. piscatorius as distributed off of Mauritania. This species is reportedly expanding its range northward due to increasing water temperatures where it is now known from as far north as Greenland, as well as Iceland and northwest Europe (Møller et al. 2010).

Mauritania is the southernmost part of the range of L. piscatorius (the bulk of its southern range is within the Mediterranean), south of that, Lophius budegassa is more common where it ranges to Senegal (Duarte et al. 2001). Lophius vaillanti, a synonym of L. piscatorius, has been recorded to range from Cape Verde (Caruso 1990) to the Gulf of Guinea and south to north of Walvis Bay, Namibia (Farina et al. 2008).
documentation.population:
Lophius piscatorius was described as frequently occurring in a trawl survey conducted off the coast of Namibia between the years 1992-1996 (Hamukuaya et al. 2001), but this record from Namibia may be a misidentification of Lophius budegassa. This species is reportedly expanding its range northward due to increasing water temperatures where it is now known from as far north as Greenland, as well as Iceland and Northwest Europe (Møller et al. 2010). This species frequently occurred in a trawl survey off the Cape Verde Islands where it was identified as the synonym L. vaillanti (Menezes et al. 2004).

Catch statistics showed an overall increasing trend up until 1976 with a sharp increase from 32,012 mt to 47,364 mt (49% increase). Catch landings subsequently dropped from 47,364 mt in 1980 to 22,259 mt in 1993 representing a 53% decrease. Catch has since fluctuated with no clear trend from 1994-2011. There is currently no effort information available for L. piscatorius.

The fishery has expanded into deeper waters since the mid-1990s, areas believed to have been a refuge for adult monkfish, leading to an increased vulnerability of the stock to overexploitation (seafish.org 2012).

Aggregate catch landings for Monkfishes (Lophius spp.) were recorded from Mauritania from 1985-2011. Over the 27 years, catch landings have fluctuated until a peak in 2000 at 45 mt. Catch subsequently declined with almost zero reported catches in 2006 at 2 mt; representing a 96% decline in six years. Catch statistics have maintained very low (near zero) landings for the last five years (2006-2011).

The natural population size of this species in the Eastern Central Atlantic is unknown. This subpopulation may be naturally low compared to subpopulations in the northern parts of its distribution.
documentation.habitats:
Lophius piscatorius is a benthic fish with a maximum size of 200 cm (more common 40-60 cm) that occurs from the shoreline to the continental slope. This species occurs in shallow waters north of FAO region 34. 

The larvae of this species are pelagic (Caruso in press). Vakily et al. (2002) describe L. piscatorius as bathydemersal with a maximum size of 200 cm SL off of West Africa. Eggs are extruded in a buoyant, gelatinous ribbon that may measure more than 10 m, which results in a highly clumped distribution of eggs and newly emerged larvae (Hislop et al. 2001). Therefore, ecosystem conditions tend to have significant impacts on recruitment success (ICES Report 2012). Lophius budegassa and L. piscatorius are long-lived species with slow growth and late maturation with females achieving older age and greater size than males (25 years vs. 21 years old; Duarte et al. 2001, Landa et al. 2001, Farina et al. 2008). 

It exhibits seasonal onshore/offshore movements in response to thermal conditions, prey availability, or for spawning (Landa et al. 2001). Landa et al. (2001) also found evidence for L. piscatorius movements between the Le Danois Bank and the Cantabrian continental shelf which may indicate mixing of the northern and southern subpopulations. In a study on this species off of northern Britain, spawning occurred in deep water, the larval transition from pelagic to demersal occurred in relatively shallow water, and most recruits entered the North Sea from the north and west which indicates that juveniles may settle hundreds of kilometres from the spawning grounds (Hislop et al. 2001).

In a tag-recapture study in southern European waters, growth rate was estimated at 13.6 cm per year-1 (Landa et al. 2007). Lophius piscatorius is a sit-and-wait predator that utilizes concealment and a lure to opportunistically feed on prey items (Laurenson et al. 2004). In a study off the Shetland Islands, UK this species preyed upon a wide variety of items (mostly fish) with the main prey being Norway Pout (Trisopterus esmarkii) and Lesser Sandeel (Ammodytes marinus) and diet composition varied seasonally (Laurenson and Priede 2005). 

In a study off the Portuguese and Spanish Atlantic coasts, L. piscatorius spawned between January to June, lengths and ages at first maturity for females were 93.9 cm and 14 years, and for males 50.3 cm and six years, and the number of mature females was low (Duarte et al. 2001). In a study in the Mediterranean, L. piscatorius had a mean size at sexual maturity for females of 68.5 cm TL (Ungaro et al. 2002). In a study off the northwest coast of Scotland on this species, ripe males occurred year-round, ripe females were found between November to May, females were larger than males, and female mean length at maturity was 73 cm and males were 49 cm (Alfonso-Dias and Hislop 1996).

Maximum age of this species is 25 years and age at first maturity is 14 years. Therefore, the generation length is 18 years (25-(14/2)) and three generations is 54 years.
documentation.threats: Lophius piscatorius is targeted by bottom trawl fisheries (Caruso in press). Lophius budegassa and L. piscatorius are lumped together in the fishery off of Portugal and Spain where total allowable catch (TAC) limits were set at very high levels from 1987 to 1999 (10,000-13,000 tonnes), and did not restrict the fishery. Since 2005, the TAC has been set at 2,000 tonnes which is against recommendations by ICES which has been advocating for a moratorium (Azevedo et al. 2008). Lophius budegassa was observed in a study on the effects of trawling on deep sea coral banks in the eastern-central Mediterranean, where the results indicated significant differences in demersal fish biomass between trawled vs. non-trawled areas (D’Onghia et al. 2010). In a study of the gill net fishery off the northern coast of Spain it was estimated that 18.1 tonnes of Lophius spp. are captured annually by abandoned nets (ghost fishing) which represents 1.46% of the total commercial landings of this fishery (Sancho et al. 2003).
documentation.measures: There are no known conservation measures for Lophius piscatorius.
documentation.use_trade:
Lophius piscatorius is targeted by bottom trawl fisheries in FAO Area 34 in the Gulf of Guinea (Schneider 1990) and is considered a highly desirable foodfish in the market. Species-specific catch statistics are not available from FAO Areas 34 and 47 (Caruso in press). 

Lophius budegassa and L. piscatorius are among the most valuable fish targeted in western and southern European waters. They have occurred as bycatch in North Atlantic fisheries for at least the past century until they began to be specifically targeted there and in Iberian waters in the 1980s (Hislop et al. 2001). ICES considers there to be a northern and southern stock, however, there is some doubt whether this is true (Blanco et al. 2008). 

Lophius budegassa and L. piscatorius are targeted in bottom trawl fisheries and gill net fisheries off Portugal and Spain where the landings peaked between 1980 and 1986/1987 and have generally decreased thereafter (Farnia et al. 2008). After 2000, the number of juveniles of L. budegassa and L. piscatorius caught in the Spanish Northeast Atlantic trawl fisheries increased in most areas (Diaz et al. 2008). The North Atlantic trawl fishery for L. piscatorius and L. budegassa (composes a lesser percentage of the catch than L. piscatorius) in ICES Subarea VI (West of Scotland and Rockall) and Division IVa (the North Sea) expanded rapidly in the late 1980s and early 1990s, with landings peaking at almost 35,000 tonnes in 1996 and significant subsequent decline thereafter. Total allowable catch limits were set in 1999, however, misreporting by fishermen was suspected and probable. Stock assessment attempts lacked many valuable pieces of data (Dobby et al. 2008). There have also been declines of Lophius spp. catch in the ICES Divisions Vllb, c and j,k in Irish waters since the mid-1980s (Fahy and Gleeson 1992).

ICES advises the management of three stocks in European waters: North Sea (Divisions IIIa, IVa–c, and VIa,b), Northern (Divisions VIIb–k and VIIIa,b,d), and Iberian (Divisions VIIIc and IXa). In ICES Divisions VIIb-k and VIIIa,b,d the 2011 and 2012 TACs were 40,950 tonnes and 38,900 tonnes respectively, while the 2010 TAC for both species combined was 41,400 tonnes and estimated landings 28,880 tonnes. Spain and France together contributed about 80% of total stock landings. Since 2007 the assessment has been based on commercial landings per unit effort (LPUEs) and data from four surveys that gather data on biomass, abundance indices and length distributions. For L. piscatorius, biomass has been increasing due to very high recruitments in 2001, 2002, and 2004 and has stabilized in recent years, however, the French survey saw some decrease in the last two years. There is evidence of good recruitment in 2008-2010. In ICES Divisions VIIIc and IXa landings of both species combined were 2,331 tonnes in 2010, which was 58% above the set TAC of 1,496 tonnes. The TAC in 2011 and 2012 was 1,571 tonnes and 3,300 tonnes respectively.

The two species are assessed separately (but managed together) using a surplus-production model (software ASPIC), tuned with commercial LPUE series for L. budegassa and a length based SS3 implementation for L. piscatorius. Biomass of L. piscatorius decreased during the 1980s and early 1990s, but has increased over the last two decades to around 7,500 tonnes. Fishing mortality peaked during the late 1980s but has since declined and is currently stable and close to FMSY (0.19). Recruitment has been relatively low in recent years and shows little evidence of strong year classes since 2001. It is particularly difficult to manage these stocks due to the lack of ageing data and further study on growth is needed (ICES Report 2012). Farina et al. (2008) also indicates there is a need for a better understanding of the location of spawning grounds and related behaviour.
documentation.rationale: Lophius piscatorius is restricted to the eastern Atlantic from Greenland to Mauritania, including the Mediterranean, however, there is some question as to whether it ranges even further south to Namibia. It is a demersal species that can occur from the shore to the continental slope. It is a long-lived, late-maturing, slow-growing species with fluctuating levels of recruitment that may make it susceptible to overfishing. It is heavily targeted by bottom trawl fisheries in the North Atlantic where overfishing and habitat destruction has been documented. It is regulated by ICES which recommends a moratorium. It is listed as Least Concern.
